headline: Covfefe
dek: Six words, one of which does not exist. The post stayed up for hours. A real president would have issued a correction; Fribourg and the Nord have other explanations.

original.speaker: Donald J. Trump
text: Despite the constant negative press covfefe
original.context: Posted shortly after midnight, Washington time, and deleted several hours later. The White House press secretary, Sean Spicer, later said that the President and a small group of people knew exactly what he meant.

verification.note: Check the exact time of posting and deletion against the archive before launch.

en: Despite persistent criticism in the press, my administration remains focused on the work the American people elected us to do. A free press is entitled to its criticism, and we are entitled to answer it with results.
Correction: an earlier message from this account was sent incomplete. We regret the error.
fr: Malgré les critiques persistantes de la presse, mon administration reste concentrée sur la mission que les Américains lui ont confiée. Une presse libre a le droit de critiquer ; nous avons le devoir de répondre par des résultats.
Rectificatif : un précédent message de ce compte a été publié incomplet. Nous prions nos lecteurs de nous en excuser.
changes: Treats the press as a fact of democracy rather than an enemy.
Corrects the mistake instead of letting the spokesman explain it.

fr: Salut les gaillards ! Malgré tout ce que les journaux racontent sur moi à longueur de journée… covfefe.

Bon. Ceux d’en dehors du canton ont cru à une faute de frappe. Mais chez nous, en Gruyère, après une Bénichon, trois verres de vin et la moutarde de Bénichon, tout le monde parle comme ça, et personne ne demande de traduction.
D’ailleurs, de l’autre côté de la Sarine, ils ont compris tout de suite. Ils ont dit « Genau ». Allez, on finit la moitié-moitié avant qu’elle refroidisse.
en: Hey folks! Despite everything the papers say about me all day long… covfefe.

Now, people from outside the canton thought it was a typo. But here in Gruyère, after a harvest festival, three glasses of wine and the festival’s sweet mustard, everybody talks like that, and nobody asks for a translation.
Besides, across the river, in the German-speaking part, they got it right away. They said “Exactly.” Come on, let’s finish the fondue before it gets cold.
notes: The Bénichon is Fribourg’s autumn harvest festival: a meal of many courses served with a sweet, spiced “moutarde de Bénichon”.
The Sarine river roughly marks the language border: French on one bank, German on the other. “Genau” means “exactly”.
Moitié-moitié (“half and half”) is the Fribourg fondue: half Gruyère, half Vacherin fribourgeois.

fr: Eh biloute ! Malgré tous chés journalisses qui dis’tent du mal ed mi tout l’temps… covfefe.
Ch’est pas un mot, ch’est un éternuement. Avec l’drache qu’on a eue toute la semaine, t’aurais été enrhumé aussi.
Allez, viens boire un jus à la maison, on va pas en faire un fromage. Même pas un maroilles.
en: Hey, buddy! Despite all those journalists badmouthing me all the time… covfefe.
It’s not a word, it’s a sneeze. With the downpour we’ve had all week, you’d have caught a cold too.
Come on, come over for a coffee, let’s not make a big cheese out of it. Not even a stinky one.
notes: “Biloute” is an affectionate Ch’ti word for a friend, a kid, or anyone you like.
“La drache” is a heavy downpour, a regular feature of northern French weather.
“En faire un fromage” means to make a fuss. Maroilles is the Nord’s famously pungent cheese.
In the North, “un jus” is a coffee, and an invitation home comes faster than the rain.
